facts.text: Head Waters earned its name from the headwaters of the Cowpasture River to the south and the South Fork South Branch Potomac River to the north.
Settled in the mid‑1700s, Head Waters grew around Scotch‑Irish, English, and German pioneers who established farms, mills, and livestock operations amid rugged Appalachia.
At about 2,047 feet above sea level, Head Waters ranks among the highest mean elevations east of the Mississippi River.
The community sits precisely on the Eastern Continental Divide, separating waters that flow into the James River system from those draining into the Potomac.
Early surveys in the 1740s granted tracts along the Bullpasture and Cowpasture rivers to families such as the Bodkins, Millers, and Wilsons, who cleared woodlands for homesteads.
Before European colonization, Native Americans, especially the Shawnee, used the Head Waters area as a hunting ground and transit route across the Potomac watershed.
